title: Rising Aerosol Burdens in the Warm Desert City of Phoenix, AZ: Hydroclimatic–LULC Drivers and Exposure Disparities in a Climate–Land Surface–Society Framework
content:
Abstract

Desert cities in the U.S. Southwest experience the nation's highest aerosol burdens, but how air pollution co-evolves with hydroclimatic–LULC metrics and racial/ethnic exposure dynamics remains unclear. We developed 30 m Landsat-derived summer aerosol optical depth (AOD) (2000–2020) for Phoenix, used explainable machine learning to attribute AOD trends to land-surface changes, and linked them to racial/ethnic disparities. We computed pixel-wise Sen's slope for AOD, land surface temperature (LST), actual evapotranspiration (ETa), and NDVI, and derived LULC transitions. These Sen's slope metrics were aggregated to census block groups to explore racial/ethnic exposure disparities. Random Forest with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) quantified contributions of hydroclimatic-LULC changes to AOD trends. Results show citywide AOD rose, shifting from very clean to moderate/elevated levels with concentrations in the urban core and rapidly urbanizing corridors, opposite national declines. NDVI slope decrease (greenness loss) was the main driver of AOD increases, followed by ETa decline (surface moisture loss). LST effects were context-dependent, and LULC transitions further amplify AOD increases. SHAP dependence curves revealed threshold-and-saturation dynamics, where near-zero NDVI/ETa slopes, small positive shifts rapidly reduce AOD slope, but the benefits flattened at higher ETa gains. Racial/ethnic minority communities are disproportionately located in low NDVI/ETa, high LST regimes and experience higher AOD and steeper increases, yet also occupy high-leverage zones where improving vegetation cover and surface moisture can produce disproportionate reductions in AOD. This integrated climate-land surface-society framework supports equity-centered, threshold-saturation-aware actions that prioritize limited resources in high-leverage zones to achieve co-benefits for air quality and environmental justice.
